userPrompt: What obligations does a data processor have under GDPR versus a data controller?
responseText:
**Key distinction under GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)**

- **Data Controller**: Determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data (Art. 4(7)). Bears primary responsibility.
- **Data Processor**: Processes personal data on behalf of the controller (Art. 4(8)). Acts only on documented instructions.

### Obligations of a Data Controller
The controller is ultimately accountable for compliance. Main obligations include:

- Lawful basis for processing (Art. 6, 9).
- Transparency: provide privacy notices to data subjects (Arts. 12–14).
- Data subject rights: facilitate access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection (Arts. 15–22).
- Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) where high risk (Art. 35).
- Prior consultation with supervisory authority when required (Art. 36).
- Maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30).
- Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures (Art. 24, 32).
- Ensure contracts with processors comply with Art. 28.
- Breach notification: to supervisory authority within 72h (Art. 33) and, where appropriate, to data subjects (Art. 34).
- Demonstrate accountability (Art. 5(2)).

### Obligations of a Data Processor
The processor’s duties are narrower and flow from the controller’s instructions and the binding contract:

- Process only on documented instructions from the controller (Art. 28(3)(a)); inform controller if an instruction infringes GDPR.
- Ensure confidentiality: bind all persons with access to data to confidentiality (Art. 28(3)(b), 32).
- Implement appropriate security measures (Art. 32).
- Assist the controller in fulfilling data subject rights (Art. 28(3)(e)).
- Assist the controller with DPIAs, breach notifications, and supervisory consultations (Art. 28(3)(f)).
- Maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30(2)).
- Notify the controller without undue delay of any personal data breach (Art. 33(2)).
- Delete or return all data at the end of the processing (Art. 28(3)(g)).
- Allow audits and inspections by the controller or its auditor (Art. 28(3)(h)).
- Ensure any sub-processor is bound by the same obligations via a written contract (Art. 28(4)).

### Summary of Differences
| Aspect                      | Controller                          | Processor                              |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Primary responsibility      | Full compliance & accountability    | Compliance with instructions & contract|
| Lawful basis & transparency | Direct duty                         | None (controller’s duty)               |
| Data subject rights         | Primary obligation to respond       | Duty to assist                         |
| Breach notification         | To SA & data subjects               | Only to controller                     |
| Records of processing       | Full records                        | Records of its own processing          |
| DPIA & prior consultation   | Must carry out / consult            | Must assist                            |
| Contract with other parties | Signs processor agreements          | Signs sub-processor agreements         |

Controllers cannot delegate their core accountability. Processors become controllers (and jointly liable) if they exceed instructions or determine purposes (Art. 28(10), Art. 82).

For legal advice on a specific situation, consult a qualified data protection lawyer.
